zh.question: 海里的水变成云以后，还能回到海里吗？每一份水都走同一条路吗？
zh.observe: 先在同一三维流域追踪100份水，比较干湿空气、透水土壤、紧实黏土与铺装面。云内放大与山坡孔隙剖面保留这批水的编号和进度；切换视角不会清空历史。再从解说中的长期观察入口进入地下水收支，或多年积雪与冰川实验，比较补给与取水、积累与消融。长期实验有独立预算与时钟，不与主场景的100份水相加。

academic.title: 能量推动相变
academic.body: 太阳辐射为蒸发提供重要的能量来源，液面上的部分水分子进入空气；蒸发在没有沸腾时也会发生。空气冷却到合适条件后，水汽可在微小颗粒上凝结。可见的云由许多液滴、冰晶或两者组成，气态水本身不可见。凝结释放潜热，与蒸发吸热共同联系着水循环和大气能量收支。

academic.title: 重力连接不同水库
academic.body: 相同降水落在不同地表，进入孔隙、沿表面流动和暂留的份额可能不同。本页用固定教学比例进行对比；真实结果还取决于降雨强度、地面坡度、前期含水量、结构和裂隙。水沿可见坡面小沟进入同一河谷，经湖泊和湖口到海；河床、水面和追踪路线共享地形。入渗水再经过非饱和土层才可能补给含水层，入渗并不等于已成为地下水。地下水主要在连通孔隙和裂隙中流动，并非普遍存在的地下空洞河流；水头差决定它可能补给河流，也可能从河流获得水。长期实验另用简化储水箱核对补给、交换、取水与储量变化，不计算真实三维流场或水质净化。

academic.title: 冰川是慢储存，不是冻住的河水
academic.body: 山地冰川形成需要积雪多次越夏保留，并逐渐转为粒雪和冰。压实减少体积，不会凭空删除水量，所以长期实验用水当量统一记账。积累与消融之差决定净收支；持续净损失可使末端后退，但冰本身仍可向下游移动。上方追踪一批水在既有冰川中的运动；下方实验另算多年雪、粒雪与冰的简化收支，不把两个数量混为一谈。末端形状和教学年份没有按真实冰川标定，也不是完整应力变形或气候预测。

zh.misconception: 云不是一袋看不见的水汽；我们看见的是许多微小水滴或冰晶。
zh.boundary: 100份批次不是全球水量比例、实测降水或完整流域水量平衡。主景按水份当前的教学位置计数；地形、云体、颗粒、孔隙与时间不按同一真实比例，河湖水面不由批次计数驱动。云下暖层融化成雨与高山降雪是两条支路。主景的既有冰体慢时间，以及长期地下水和冰川实验各有独立预算与时间尺，不能混加，也不能用于当地水位、冰川或气候预测。不模拟完整三维含水层、冰川应力变形、污染净化或植物蒸腾。

narration.label: 从一片海开始
narration.text: 你见过雨后慢慢变干的地面吗？水没有被地面吃掉，有一些变成了看不见的水蒸气，走进空气。海面也在发生这样的事。阳光送来能量，水的旅行就可以继续。画面里的金色圆圈像一支小指示笔，帮助我们追踪其中一小份水。

narration.label: 来到云里
narration.text: 空气里的水汽在合适的条件下凝结成小水滴，云就变得看得见了。放大同一片云，会看到小水滴相遇后合并。有些云也有冰晶。云不保证把雨送到地面：如果下面的空气很干，雨滴可能在途中重新变成水蒸气。
narration.cue: 推进至云中，留出三秒观察。

narration.label: 雨落下来
narration.text: 云里的小颗粒还要继续长大，才可能成为落下来的雨或雪。这一回，我们跟着雨来到山坡。水受到地球的吸引，沿着地面往低处走，小溪和河流把一些水送回大海。看看圆圈经过的弯弯河道，水可不是一下子跳回海里的。
narration.cue: 慢慢推进经过雨和河道。

narration.label: 留下很久的水
narration.text: 不同的水走不同的路。有的进入土和石头的小缝隙，慢慢补给河流；有的以雪落在高山。把时间拉长，留下来的雪可以逐渐变成冰。冰也会慢慢向下移动。如果损失的水比新来的更多，冰川会变小，地下储存的水也会减少。水的旅程没有规定好的终点，有些变化值得慢慢看。
narration.cue: 先看批次中的冰与融水；再进入两个独立长期实验，分别比较地下水补给/取水与冰川积累/消融，保持时间尺和数量边界可见。

en.question: Can seawater return to the sea after becoming a cloud? Does every portion take the same route?
en.observe: Track 100 portions in the same 3D watershed and compare humid or dry air, permeable soil, compact clay and paving. Cloud magnification and the hillside pore section retain batch identities and progress; camera changes preserve history. Then use the longer-term entries in the explanation panel to compare groundwater recharge with pumping, or snow accumulation with glacier loss. Those studies have independent budgets and clocks and are not added to the 100 portions.

academic.title: Energy and changes of state
academic.body: Solar radiation supplies much of the energy for evaporation, which also occurs below boiling. Cooling can allow vapor to condense on tiny particles. Visible clouds contain droplets, ice crystals or both; gaseous water is invisible. Evaporation absorbs latent heat and condensation releases it, linking water movement to atmospheric energy.

academic.title: Gravity connects water stores
academic.body: The same rain can partition differently between infiltration, surface runoff and temporary storage on different surfaces. This page compares fixed teaching fractions; real outcomes also depend on rainfall intensity, slope, previous moisture, structure and cracks. Water follows the visible hillside rill into the same valley, lake and outlet; bed, water and tracer routes share one geometry. Infiltrated water may later pass through unsaturated soil to recharge an aquifer, so infiltration is not already recharge. Groundwater travels through connected pores and fractures rather than a universal cavern river. Hydraulic-head differences can make it feed a river or receive river water. The separate long-term experiment balances recharge, exchange, pumping and storage in simplified boxes; it does not calculate real 3D flow or water purification.

academic.title: Glaciers store water on slower timescales
academic.body: Mountain glaciers require snow to survive repeated summers and gradually become firn and ice. Compaction reduces volume without deleting water, so the longer-term experiment uses water equivalent for its budget. Accumulation minus loss gives the net balance. Sustained losses can make the terminus retreat while ice still moves downstream. Above, a batch travels through an existing glacier; below, a separate model balances snow, firn and ice over teaching years. Those quantities must not be combined. Terminus geometry and years are uncalibrated, not a full stress, deformation or climate prediction.

en.misconception: A cloud is not a bag of invisible vapor: its visible parts are tiny droplets or ice crystals.
en.boundary: The 100 portions are not global water proportions, measured rainfall or a complete catchment water balance. The main scene counts current teaching locations; terrain, clouds, tracers, pores and time use different illustrative scales, and batch counts do not drive river or lake levels. Ice melting into rain in a warm layer below a cloud is distinct from high-mountain snowfall. The existing glacier’s slow batch clock and the longer-term groundwater and glacier studies have separate budgets and time scales. They cannot be combined or used for local water-level, glacier or climate forecasts. Full 3D aquifer flow, glacier stress and deformation, contaminant purification and plant transpiration are not simulated.

narration.label: Start at the sea
narration.text: Have you seen wet ground slowly dry after rain? The ground has not eaten the water. Some has become invisible water vapor and entered the air. This happens over the sea too. Sunshine supplies energy for the journey. Our gold circle is a little pointer helping us follow one portion of water.
narration.cue: Point to the sea and pause for two seconds.

narration.label: Into a cloud
narration.text: Under suitable conditions, water vapor condenses into droplets and the cloud becomes visible. Enlarging the same cloud shows droplets meeting and merging. Some clouds also contain ice. A cloud does not guarantee rain at the ground: very dry air below can turn the falling rain back into vapor.
narration.cue: Advance into the cloud and pause for three seconds.

narration.label: Rain falls
narration.text: The tiny particles in clouds must grow before they can fall as rain or snow. This time we follow rain onto a hillside. Earth pulls water downward, and streams and rivers carry some back to the sea. Watch the circle travel along the winding river: the water does not simply jump back into the ocean.
narration.cue: Advance slowly through rainfall and along the river.

narration.label: Water that stays longer
narration.text: Different portions take different routes. Some enter little spaces in soil and rock and slowly feed a river. Some fall as snow high in the mountains. Over a longer time, snow that stays can gradually become ice. Ice moves slowly downhill too. If more water is lost than arrives, a glacier gets smaller, and underground water stores can shrink too. Water has no compulsory final stop. Some changes are worth watching slowly.
narration.cue: First compare batch ice and meltwater, then enter the two independent longer-term studies: groundwater recharge versus withdrawal and glacier accumulation versus loss. Keep separate clocks and quantities visible.
